title: US Senator Introduces Bill to Freeze H-1B Visas for Three Years and Codify $100,000 Fee
excerpt: Montana Republican Tim Sheehy's 'End H-1B Abuse Act' seeks to pause new visas and enshrine the fee that courts have struck down.
body:
• Senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana) introduced the 'End H-1B Abuse Act' seeking a three-year moratorium on new H-1B visa issuances
  • The bill would codify the $100,000 per-petition fee that a federal appeals court blocked just days earlier as an unlawful tax
  • After the pause, the programme would restart under tighter limits, higher standards and strengthened fraud protections
  • The H-1B programme issues 85,000 visas annually, with Indian nationals accounting for the overwhelming majority of recipients

A Republican senator has introduced legislation that would halt the issuance of new H-1B visas for three years and write the Trump administration's $100,000 filing fee into law — a move that would deal a severe blow to Indian technology workers who dominate the programme.

What the Bill Proposes

Senator Tim Sheehy of Montana introduced the "End H-1B Abuse Act" on Thursday, calling it "a critical, proactive step" to protect American workers, curb H-1B fraud and address what he described as national security risks. The legislation is backed by the Federation for American Immigration Reform and the Immigration Accountability Project.

https://x.com/DeccanChronicle/status/2080900405064818740

"The H-1B programme was created to address workforce shortages for specialised, difficult-to-fill positions — not to displace qualified, hardworking Americans with cheaper, foreign labour," Sheehy said in a statement. "My legislation restores the programme to its original intent and puts American workers first by closing loopholes that incentivise abuse."

The bill would freeze all new H-1B visa issuances for three years, after which the programme would restart under tighter limits and higher eligibility standards. It would also codify the $100,000 fee for each H-1B petition — the same fee that federal courts have repeatedly blocked.

Timing Raises Stakes

The bill lands just days after the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Trump administration's bid to reinstate the $100,000 fee. US District Judge Leo Sorokin had ruled in June that the fee amounted to an unlawful tax Congress never authorised. The appeals court agreed, noting the administration failed to show it was likely to succeed on appeal.

"The Court finds that the Policy imposes a tax on H-1B petitions without the requisite delegation by Congress."

— US District Judge Leo Sorokin, in his June ruling striking down the fee

By moving to codify the fee through legislation, Sheehy's bill attempts to accomplish through Congress what the executive branch could not achieve unilaterally. If enacted, it would eliminate the constitutional objection that sank the executive order.

Impact on Indian Workers

The H-1B visa programme allows US companies to employ highly skilled foreign workers in speciality occupations. It issues 65,000 visas annually, with an additional 20,000 reserved for holders of advanced US degrees. Indian nationals have historically claimed roughly 70 percent of all H-1B approvals, making any restriction on the programme disproportionately consequential for Indian workers and their families.

American technology companies depend on the programme to hire tens of thousands of employees each year. Court filings in the fee case showed the $100,000 charge sharply reduced demand for new H-1B petitions even during its brief period of enforcement.

The bill faces an uncertain path in the Senate, where previous attempts to impose moratoriums on skilled-worker visas have struggled to gain bipartisan support. A parallel effort in the House — a separate bill introduced by Republican members seeking a similar three-year pause — signals growing legislative appetite for H-1B restrictions, though neither measure is guaranteed floor time in the current session.

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals on H-1B visas or waiting in the green card backlog, the legislative push adds another layer of uncertainty to an already volatile immigration landscape.
